section.title: The real line and intervals
section.p: Numbers do two jobs for us. They locate points, and they measure distances between points. The same number 3 can mean a position on a line, a length, a time, a temperature, or an error bound. Calculus depends on moving between these meanings without confusion.

subsection.title: Points as numbers
subsection.p: We picture the real numbers on a horizontal line. Positive numbers lie to the right of 0. Negative numbers lie to the left.

subsection.title: Open, closed, and half-open intervals
subsection.p: An interval is an unbroken piece of the real line. If two numbers are in the interval, then every number between them is also in the interval.

subsection.p: There are also infinite intervals:
The symbols \infty and -\infty are not real numbers. They are directions. So we never write a square bracket next to \infty.

statement.p: The set of all times from 0 to 3 hours, including both endpoints, is [0,3].
The set of all positive times is (0,\infty).
The set of all nonnegative times is [0,\infty).

paragraphs.title: Why \varepsilon\gt 0 appears
paragraphs.p: The number \varepsilon is usually an allowed error. Allowed errors must be positive.
If \varepsilon=0, then |x-a|\lt 0 has no solution, because a distance cannot be negative.
If \varepsilon\lt 0, the inequality |x-a|\lt \varepsilon also has no solution.
So whenever we write |x-a|\lt \varepsilon to describe closeness, we mean \varepsilon\gt 0.

subsection.title: Inequalities as a way to control error
subsection.p: The word error does not mean a mistake. It means the difference between a quantity and the value we want.

subsection.p: The real line now gives us a way to talk about closeness. But there is a deeper question hiding under the picture. Is the line really unbroken? Are there numbers for all the points that geometry asks for?
The answer is yes for the real numbers. It is no for the rational numbers. That difference is one reason calculus is built on \mathbb{R}, not just on fractions.
